better_principle: Control direct-to-wet ratio and spatial cues, then test depth in the full mix.
myth: More reverb always means more depth.
why_it_is_misleading: Wet level can simply make a source washed out; distance also depends on direct level, pre-delay, early reflections, brightness, and context.

better_principle: Separate perceived size from decay length and choose each by role.
myth: Longer decay always makes a space sound bigger.
why_it_is_misleading: Room-size cues include reflection spacing and pre-delay; a long decay can sound like a small resonant or artificial space.

better_principle: Sweep around a musical starting point and stop before a detached slap appears.
myth: There is one correct pre-delay formula for every tempo.
why_it_is_misleading: Tempo math is only a starting orientation; articulation, room type, source rhythm, and desired separation determine the useful value.

better_principle: Filter only enough to solve an identified low-end conflict.
myth: Every reverb return must be aggressively high-passed.
why_it_is_misleading: Filtering can prevent buildup, but low-frequency room information may be musically useful and excessive cuts can make space thin.

better_principle: Choose by articulation, depth role, genre, and arrangement space.
myth: Plate is always the correct vocal reverb.
why_it_is_misleading: Plates are common but rooms, chambers, halls, delays, or no reverb may better fit the singer and arrangement.

better_principle: Choose topology by dry preservation, reuse, and control.
myth: Professional mixes always use reverb only on sends.
why_it_is_misleading: Sends are flexible, but inserts are valid for self-contained creative effects, printed assets, or source-specific wet/dry processing.

better_principle: Use a shared space only when it serves a coherent role.
myth: One shared reverb automatically glues a mix.
why_it_is_misleading: A shared room can help cohesion, but poor timing/color or excessive sends can still clutter the arrangement.

better_principle: Compare in context and value fit over category prestige.
myth: Convolution is always more realistic and therefore better.
why_it_is_misleading: An IR captures one response and may include coloration or context that does not fit; algorithmic spaces can sound more convincing musically.

better_principle: Judge articulation, color, movement, and fit.
myth: Algorithmic reverb is fake and inferior.
why_it_is_misleading: All artificial reverbs are tools; algorithmic designs can create plausible or intentionally stylized spaces with useful control.

better_principle: Use the minimum width that supports the spatial role.
myth: Wider reverb is always more immersive.
why_it_is_misleading: Extreme width can weaken center focus and mono compatibility.

better_principle: Make final timing, tone, and level decisions in the full mix.
myth: Set reverb while the source is soloed, then leave it.
why_it_is_misleading: Solo helps inspect the return but hides masking and arrangement context.

better_principle: Inspect and filter/shorten the return before reshaping the source.
myth: If reverb is muddy, EQ the dry source.
why_it_is_misleading: The wet path may be the source of buildup; altering the dry source can damage identity.

better_principle: Balance early detail, damping, level, and dry clarity.
myth: A brighter reverb is always clearer.
why_it_is_misleading: Bright tails can emphasize sibilance and cymbal splash, increasing masking.

better_principle: Control decay, density, and low-mid content, not only highs.
myth: A dark reverb is automatically invisible.
why_it_is_misleading: Dark energy can accumulate in low mids and become a cloud.

better_principle: Evaluate the whole direct/early/tail relationship.
myth: Long pre-delay always makes the source closer.
why_it_is_misleading: It can separate the dry onset, but other distance cues and audible echoes may contradict the impression.

better_principle: Meter input/output and manage send gain/headroom.
myth: Reverb cannot clip because it is diffuse and quiet.
why_it_is_misleading: Multiple sends and overlapping tails can sum to high peaks and overload auxes or buses.

better_principle: Use the lowest mode that passes listening and technical checks for the current stage.
myth: Higher quality/oversampling settings always sound better enough to justify the cost.
why_it_is_misleading: Quality modes may matter differently by algorithm and context and can impair tracking latency/CPU.

better_principle: Audition and compare onset/tail/color in context.
myth: An IR named 'large hall' guarantees a large-hall result in the mix.
why_it_is_misleading: IR labels cannot account for source, capture chain, level, timing, and arrangement.

better_principle: Choose mono or stereo by role and translation.
myth: Mono reverb is amateurish.
why_it_is_misleading: Mono returns can provide focus, vintage character, and deliberate localization.

better_principle: Protect low-frequency timing and mono focus, then experiment on upper content.
myth: Never put reverb on bass.
why_it_is_misleading: Full-band sub reverb is risky, but short/filtered/upper-band ambience can be useful.

better_principle: Address recording/source problems first, then add space if useful.
myth: Artificial reverb fixes a badly recorded room.
why_it_is_misleading: Added ambience does not remove comb filtering, noise, or problematic reflections already recorded.

better_principle: Add only spatial roles the arrangement needs.
myth: Every track needs reverb so it belongs in the mix.
why_it_is_misleading: Some sources already contain room, and deliberate dryness creates contrast and focus.

better_principle: Use tempo math as a comparison point and decide by tail clearance.
myth: A decay ending exactly on a note value is always tighter.
why_it_is_misleading: Exact timing can help but may sound forced or still mask events.

better_principle: Reset level/timing/filtering around the actual source and goal.
myth: A premium or famous reverb preset makes vocals professional.
why_it_is_misleading: The preset cannot know performance, recording, arrangement, or lyric density.

better_principle: Use measurements as supporting evidence and confirm by controlled listening.
myth: A spectrum analyzer can prove a reverb is muddy or good.
why_it_is_misleading: The analyzer describes energy but not whether the artistic space is appropriate.

better_principle: Compare synced and free timing in the actual groove.
myth: Delay should always be synchronized to tempo.
why_it_is_misleading: Off-grid or fixed-time delays can better follow human feel, slapback, or sound-design goals.

better_principle: Choose subdivisions by repeat placement, not reputation.
myth: Dotted-eighth delay automatically makes any part sound professional.
why_it_is_misleading: It works only when the performance and arrangement leave complementary accents.

better_principle: Treat feedback as a loop with safety and tail context.
myth: Feedback is just a harmless repeat-count control.
why_it_is_misleading: Feedback can accumulate filtering, distortion, noise, and energy and may become unstable.

better_principle: Check mono/correlation and compare with real doubling or ambience.
myth: The Haas effect is a free stereo widener with no downside.
why_it_is_misleading: Short offsets can create comb filtering, center shifts, and mono cancellation.

better_principle: Polarity-check and listen across multiple events and frequency regions.
myth: Aligning waveform peaks guarantees correct phase.
why_it_is_misleading: Phase relationship varies by frequency and musical event; one visual peak is not enough.

better_principle: Measure the actual path and inspect Low Latency Mode/manual offsets.
myth: Plug-in Delay Compensation fixes every timing problem.
why_it_is_misleading: PDC depends on reported latency and may not cover external, live-input, manual, or unusual routing conditions.

better_principle: Use the fewest repeats that fulfill the role.
myth: More feedback always makes delay sound bigger.
why_it_is_misleading: It often creates clutter, harmonic collisions, and headroom problems.

better_principle: Shape the wet path according to source and arrangement.
myth: Filtering repeats is only a vintage-color trick.
why_it_is_misleading: Filtering is a core way to separate repeats from the dry source and manage masking.

better_principle: Choose routing by control and dry-path needs.
myth: Delay should only ever be on an aux.
why_it_is_misleading: Auxes are flexible, but insert delay can be appropriate for self-contained effects and wet/dry sound design.

better_principle: Automate the parameter that matches the intended behavior.
myth: A delay throw is made by automating the return fader.
why_it_is_misleading: Return automation affects existing tails; send automation usually selects what enters the delay.

better_principle: Use math to orient, then nudge/listen.
myth: 60,000/BPM gives the one correct delay time.
why_it_is_misleading: It gives a quarter-note starting value, not the best groove or subdivision.

better_principle: Choose spatial behavior by source role.
myth: Stereo delay is always better than mono delay.
why_it_is_misleading: Stereo movement can distract or collapse; mono repeats can focus and translate well.

better_principle: Keep low-band timing/mono focus controlled and scope the effect.
myth: Never use delay on bass or 808.
why_it_is_misleading: Sub repeats are risky, but filtered upper-band or transition-specific delays can be useful.

better_principle: Compare both in mono and stereo.
myth: A short delay is the same as real double tracking.
why_it_is_misleading: A delayed copy has identical pitch, articulation, and performance, unlike a true second take.

better_principle: Balance dry center, repeat level, and mono behavior.
myth: Ping-pong delay always creates useful width.
why_it_is_misleading: Alternating repeats can empty the center or overload side space.

better_principle: Level-match and check placement through the next event.
myth: If the delay makes the groove feel stronger, the timing must be correct.
why_it_is_misleading: Higher wet level can create excitement even when repeats collide.

better_principle: Make final decisions in full context.
myth: Set delay in solo and trust it.
why_it_is_misleading: The effect’s usefulness depends on gaps, chords, lyrics, and other rhythmic layers.

better_principle: Check every chord/section the tail crosses.
myth: Delay is rhythmic, so harmony does not matter.
why_it_is_misleading: Repeats carry pitch into later chords and can create dissonance.

better_principle: Start low, limit output, and maintain an immediate mute.
myth: Any effects can be placed in the feedback loop safely.
why_it_is_misleading: Resonant EQ, pitch, saturation, and gain can grow rapidly with feedback.

better_principle: Edit/perform at the right timescale and use offsets only for consistent displacement.
myth: Sample or region delay can fix a bad performance automatically.
why_it_is_misleading: Global offsets cannot correct internal timing inconsistency or articulation.

better_principle: Choose repeat behavior and tone by role.
myth: Tape delay is inherently warmer and better than digital delay.
why_it_is_misleading: Color is contextual; noise, modulation, filtering, and saturation can help or harm.

better_principle: Compare both at matched spatial impression.
myth: Delay is always a cleaner substitute for reverb.
why_it_is_misleading: Discrete repeats may be more distracting or rhythmically dense than a short diffuse room.

better_principle: Blend from zero in context.
myth: A specific wet percentage works across all delay setups.
why_it_is_misleading: Insert/send topology, source level, feedback, and return gain change the meaning of wet percentage.

better_principle: Use the grid as evidence and confirm with listening.
myth: A waveform or timing grid can prove a delay grooves.
why_it_is_misleading: Visual placement cannot establish musical feel or distraction.

better_principle: Treat delay as arrangement and validate by section.
myth: One delay value should stay fixed for the entire song.
why_it_is_misleading: Different sections, tempos, densities, and roles may need automation or separate returns.
